newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia, Indonesia in small-lot buying of corn.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia, Indonesia in small-lot buying of corn.

text.p: Malaysia and Indonesia were said to have bought small cargoes of Chinese corn, but regional business was quiet and the impact of the Taiwan pork crisis appears to be dying down, regional traders said on Tuesday.

"We heard that the Malaysians bought about 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes of Chinese corn for May shipment. I understand the price was around (US$)149 or $150 (a tonne C&F)," a trader for a U.S. commodity trading house told Reuters.

Another dealer for a commodity house in Singapore said the "Indonesians also bought some corn from China in the last two weeks for around $148-$153" a tonne C&F. Delivery date was pegged for May/June.
"I think the Malaysians would continue buying but not on the same level as before," one trader said.

Most traders said the brisk corn-buying by Indonesia and Malaysia appeared to be dying down with most buyers sitting back ahead of the Easter holidays when grain futures markets will be closed in the United States and Europe.
Both countries are estimated to have bought well over 150,000 tonnes of corn each over the past few weeks with the bulk of the material coming from China and a chunk from Argentina.
"There was a pretty good round of buying. It's all pretty much Argentine or the stuff out of China," one dealer said, adding interest among regional buyers appears to be fading.
Thailand, where one flour firm bought 50,000 tonnes of Argentine corn for prompt shipment last week, was also said to be looking for several cargoes of corn, the traders said.
U.S. corn is out of the picture because of its higher price when compared to Argentine or Chinese origins, dealers said.
Argentine corn coming into Southeast Asia was seen by the trade at $150-$151 a tonne C&F for May/June shipment on board a Panamax against $150-$153 a tonne on the same basis last week.
Chinese corn in the region fetched a quote of $150-$152 a tonne C&F for May/June shipment on a Handy vessel, almost unchanged from last week's $150-$153 a tonne C&F.
U.S. corn, however, was seen by dealers at $155-$157 a tonne C&F for May/June shipment on a Panamax, slightly easier when compared to last week's $157-$158 a tonne C&F.
"The July/August positions for corn are open in the region, but the people here not in a hurry to buy," a dealer said.
The soymeal business, however, has been quiet with buyers sidelined by the high level of prices in the Chicago futures market.
HOwever, regional dealers said positions were beginning to come up and countries in the area may have no choice but to enter the market soon.
"People are paralysed in the market. But all the medium sized buyers are short," a trader for a European dealing house said.
"I think the Indonesians still need about 100,000 tonnes of meal, but they're not buying because they think the price will come down," a dealer for a U.S. commodity house said.

U.S. meal was still seen at prohibitively expensive levels, with the May/June shipment seen at $347-$348 a tonne C&F on a Panamax compared with Brazilian meal quoted at $320-$330 a tonne C&F for the same shipment period, dealers said.

The majority of the trade has already written off any residual impact on prices from the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Taiwan, which virtually wrecked the multi-billion dollar pork export industry there.
One dealer said: "What the trade is interested in is the long-term effect of the crisis, but that won't come out for quite a while."
The Asian grains and oilseeds business will probably lapse into a more quiet phase going into the Easter holidays later in the week which would shut down markets in the U.S. and Europe.
"We should get pretty quiet from tomorrow onwards," a dealer said.
